title: Incident-Guided Spatiotemporal Traffic Forecasting

problem.claim: Traffic forecasting methods need to model how suddenly occurring transportation incidents alter traffic-system dynamics and temporal patterns.

gap.claim: Most existing work focuses on historical spatiotemporal traffic dependencies and overlooks external incident disturbances, whose unpredictability makes historical patterns difficult to observe.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes the Incident-Guided Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (IGSTGNN) framework.
IGSTGNN models incident effects using Incident-Context Spatial Fusion for initial heterogeneous spatial influence and Temporal Incident Impact Decay for subsequent dynamic dissipation.
The paper constructs and releases a large-scale dataset with incident records time-aligned to traffic time series.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe IGSTGNN as a novel framework.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report state-of-the-art performance for IGSTGNN on the new benchmark.
The authors report that the ICSF and TIID modules generalize when integrated into various existing models.

narrative_sequence.summary: Deep-learning and graph-neural-network methods have rapidly developed for traffic forecasting.
Existing methods overlook incident-driven disturbances, which substantially alter temporal patterns and are difficult to learn from historical sequences.
The paper introduces IGSTGNN with spatial-fusion and temporal-decay modules for incident impacts.
A large-scale incident-aligned traffic dataset is constructed and released.
The authors report state-of-the-art benchmark performance and module generalizability across existing models.

source_observation.claim: Sudden incidents can act as external disturbances that substantially alter traffic temporal patterns.

interpretation.claim: Forecasting systems may need explicit exogenous-event modeling rather than relying only on historical traffic sequences.

application.claim: For other forecasting domains with abrupt external shocks, represent both the initial spatial or contextual effect and its subsequent temporal dissipation.

exception.claim: This lesson may not apply when external disturbances are negligible, unavailable, or do not materially change the target dynamics.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide quantitative performance values, comparison baselines, or dataset size.
The abstract does not specify incident categories, model architecture details, or validation procedures.
